Winter Riding Preparation

Riding through a British winter is demanding but achievable with proper preparation. Cold, wet, dark conditions challenge both rider and machine, but thousands of UK riders commute and tour year-round. Here's how to prepare for the cold months.

Bike Preparation

  • Tyres: Check tread depth — cold weather reduces grip, so you need maximum tread. Some riders fit softer compound tyres for winter.
  • Lighting: Ensure all lights work perfectly. Consider auxiliary lights or fog lights for murky conditions. Keep headlights clean — road spray obscures them quickly.
  • Battery: Cold weather strains batteries. Test yours and replace if it's struggling. Keep it on a trickle charger when not riding.
  • Corrosion protection: Apply ACF-50 or XCP Rust Blocker to bare metal, electrical connections, and the underside of the bike. Road salt destroys unprotected surfaces.
  • Chain maintenance: Lubricate more frequently in winter. Wet, gritty conditions strip chain lube rapidly.

Rider Gear

  • Heated gear: Heated grips are essential. Heated gloves, jacket liners, and socks move from luxury to necessity in deep winter.
  • Layering system: Base layer (merino wool), mid-layer (fleece or down), outer layer (waterproof textile suit). Adjust layers for conditions.
  • Visibility: Wear high-vis over your riding gear. In grey, wet conditions, visibility to other road users is your first line of defence.
  • Anti-fog: Pinlock visor inserts are essential. Fogging up in traffic is dangerous.
  • Waterproof over-suit: Even with a waterproof riding suit, an over-suit provides an extra layer of rain protection and warmth.

Riding Technique Adjustments

  • Smooth inputs: Cold tyres, wet roads, and reduced grip demand smoother acceleration, braking, and cornering inputs.
  • Increased stopping distance: Allow at least double the dry-weather stopping distance.
  • Road surface awareness: White lines, manhole covers, metal plates, diesel spills, and painted markings are all more slippery in cold/wet conditions.
  • Ice awareness: If temperature is below 3°C, assume ice is possible. Shaded areas, bridges, and north-facing roads ice first.
  • Visor management: Keep it clean, keep it clear. Opening the visor slightly at low speeds prevents fogging.
Winter riding is a skill that develops with practice. Start with short rides in mild winter conditions and gradually extend as you build confidence. By your second winter, you'll wonder what all the fuss was about.

When NOT to Ride in Winter

  • Temperatures below -2°C (ice risk is too high)
  • Active snowfall or ice warnings
  • Freezing rain or sleet
  • Dense fog (visibility below 50m)
  • Severe wind warnings

Route Planning for Winter Conditions

Winter routes should prioritise gritted main roads and completely avoid exposed mountain passes and high-altitude roads. The difference between a sheltered valley road and an exposed hilltop route in winter can be 5-10 degrees Celsius and represent the critical difference between clear dry tarmac and invisible black ice. Study your local council's published gritting routes — these are the safest roads available in cold weather conditions.

Carry a fully charged phone with the What3Words app installed and tested. If you break down in poor winter conditions on a remote road, being able to communicate your precise three-word location to breakdown services becomes critically important when visibility is reduced and familiar landmarks are obscured by snow, fog, or driving rain.
keyTakeaways: Riding a British winter is achievable with proper preparation of both bike and rider.
Prepare the bike with good tyre tread, perfect lighting, a healthy battery, ACF-50 corrosion protection and frequent chain lubrication.
Rider kit centres on heated grips, a layering system, high-vis, a Pinlock insert and a waterproof over-suit.
Adjust technique with smooth inputs, at least double the dry stopping distance and constant ice awareness below 3C.
Do not ride below -2C, in active snow or ice warnings, freezing rain, dense fog or severe wind warnings.

faq.q: How do I prepare my motorcycle for winter?
faq.a: Check tyre tread depth because cold weather reduces grip and you need maximum tread, and some riders fit softer compound tyres. Ensure all lights work perfectly and stay clean, test the battery and keep it on a trickle charger, and apply ACF-50 or XCP Rust Blocker to bare metal and electrical connections against road salt. Lubricate the chain more frequently as wet, gritty conditions strip lube rapidly.

faq.q: What gear do I need for winter riding?
faq.a: Heated grips are essential, with heated gloves, jacket liners and socks moving from luxury to necessity in deep winter. Use a layering system of merino base layer, fleece or down mid-layer and a waterproof textile outer. Wear high-vis over your gear, fit a Pinlock visor insert against fogging, and add a waterproof over-suit for extra rain protection and warmth.

faq.q: How should I adjust my riding technique in winter?
faq.a: Use smooth acceleration, braking and cornering inputs because cold tyres, wet roads and reduced grip are unforgiving. Allow at least double the dry-weather stopping distance. Be aware that white lines, manhole covers, metal plates, diesel spills and painted markings are all more slippery in cold, wet conditions, and if the temperature is below 3C assume ice is possible, especially on shaded areas, bridges and north-facing roads.

faq.q: When should I not ride in winter?
faq.a: Avoid riding when temperatures are below -2C because ice risk is too high, during active snowfall or ice warnings, in freezing rain or sleet, in dense fog with visibility below 50m, or during severe wind warnings. Winter riding is a skill that develops with practice, so start with short rides in mild winter conditions and gradually extend as you build confidence.

faq.q: How do I plan a safe winter route?
faq.a: Winter routes should prioritise gritted main roads and completely avoid exposed mountain passes and high-altitude roads. The difference between a sheltered valley road and an exposed hilltop can be 5-10C and the difference between clear tarmac and invisible black ice, so study your council's published gritting routes. Carry a charged phone with the What3Words app so breakdown services can find you if visibility is poor.
